def: A stated paid leave allowance beyond the statutory minimum.
Paid leave for a new parent, beyond the statutory minimum, usually stated in weeks.
A share of the company: options, RSUs, or a profit-participation scheme.
Employer-funded medical cover. The largest non-salary line in US postings; elsewhere it usually tops up public cover.
You choose when you work, within reason: flexitime, no core hours, or async by default.
The employer pays into your retirement account on top of your own contribution. The match rate is the number that matters.
A stated annual sum for courses, books, and training you choose.
Variable pay on top of salary: annual, performance, or company-wide.
Eye tests and glasses paid or subsidised, usually bundled with medical and dental.
Counselling, therapy sessions, or a subscribed service such as Headspace or Spill.
A death-in-service payout to a nominated beneficiary, typically a multiple of salary.
A recurring allowance for gym, fitness, or wellbeing spending, paid whether or not you use a specific provider.
Dental treatment paid or subsidised by the employer, usually bundled with medical cover.
Pay tied to what you sell or close, on top of base salary.
Staff pricing on the company's own products, or a perks platform with third-party discounts.
A transit pass, parking, mileage, or a cycle-to-work scheme.
Coffee, drinks, and snacks provided at the office. The smallest perk that postings still list.
Buying company stock at a discount through payroll.
A named mentor, structured buddy scheme, or paid coaching.
The role can be done at reduced hours, or a job share is on the table.
Money or logistics for moving to the job's location.
Income protection if illness or injury stops you working, short or long term.
No fixed leave allowance. Read it carefully: unlimited policies often produce less leave taken, not more.
The employer pays toward a degree, certification, or course fees.
A one-off or recurring allowance for the desk, chair, and hardware you work from.
Exam fees, study leave, and materials for a professional credential.
Cover for fertility treatment, egg freezing, surrogacy, or adoption costs.
The employer will sponsor a work permit. Only counted when the posting never declines it.
Nursery places, a childcare allowance, or back-up care when arrangements fail.
Company-paid offsites, usually annual, often somewhere the team flies to.
A stated allowance of days working from another country each year.
A specific, stated office quality: central location, roof terrace, showers, quiet rooms.
Paid absence when you are ill, stated as a policy rather than a statutory floor.
Extended paid or unpaid leave after a qualifying period, usually measured in months.
You pick the machine and peripherals, rather than taking the standard issue.
Free or subsidised food at work: lunch, canteen, or a meal card.
Your birthday as an extra paid day, or a floating personal day.
Paid attendance at industry conferences, sometimes with speaking support.
Paid days off to do charity or community work.
Additional cover the employer pays for: accident, travel, legal, or supplementary health.
A published progression ladder with levels and criteria, rather than ad-hoc promotion.
Paid time to care for a dependent adult, or bereavement leave beyond the statutory minimum.
Dogs in the office, or a pet insurance contribution.
A payment for introducing someone the company then hires.
A compressed or genuinely shortened week: 32 hours, four days, or a nine-day fortnight.
Employer-paid screening: annual physicals, eye tests for screen users, or on-site clinics.
A one-off payment for joining, sometimes tied to staying a minimum term.
